description:
These pictures are of a silver maple tree which I found in my back yard. I noticed that the backside of this leaf has a grey/silver color to it, which was one of the reasons I was able to identify this as a silver maple tree. Through more of my observations, the leaves are five lobed, with 3 major lobes. According the the source I have linked below, during the fall time, the silver maple will turn the color yellow. But for leaves that are in the full sun, they could turn red or even orange. 

This tree has a very shallow root system and "can buckle pavements, invade pipes, and prevent almost anything except grass from growing under the trees". This tree is also known to lose its lower limbs during the winter months if there are are any ice or wind storms. These facts are true because I have observed these effects happening in my own back yard. The roots of this tree are extremely shallow and are seen above the ground. During the ice storm this past winter, the silver maple's branches also broke off.

Silver maple samaras are large and straw-colored (Photo 2, lower pair), whereas red maple samaras are usually smaller and are an attractive, soft rosy shade (Photo 2, upper pair). The birds and chipmunks enjoy eating the seeds regardless of type.

ID - Silver Maple (Acer saccharinum) - Leaves are simple and grow oppositely on the stem. The terminal and lateral buds are rounded and red or reddish-brown. Seeds form in a pair of winged seeds which are called samaras, these samaras are 1" to 2" in length. Silver maple forms a broad, rounded crown. The bark of young branches will be smooth and varying in color from reddish to yellow-gray. On older branches, bark will appear dark gray and broken into long flakes or scales

It is not recommended for these trees to be planted in street boulevards because they have softwood and are prone to decay. In the wild, they grow along rivers and on floodplains; this is a tree that likes getting their feet wet. Best if planted in a yard, park, or low spot.
